ap_calculus_ab-m25.stem: In a laboratory, the temperature $T$ (in degrees C) of a sample placed in a water bath at time $t$ minutes is modeled by a differential equation. The table gives the slope of the slope-field segment $\frac{dT}{dt}$ at each grid point $(t,T)$. Which differential equation produces this slope field?

stimulus.description: Table of slope-field segment slopes dT/dt at grid points for a sample's temperature T (degrees C) in a water bath, time t in minutes.

data.units: slope in degrees C per minute

options.why: Correct: gives 1, 0, -1 at T=10, 20, 30 for every t, matching the table.
Sign error: gives -1 at T=10 and +1 at T=30, the opposite of the table.
Confuses the variables: slope would depend on t (2, 1.9, 1.8) and would be the same for every T, but the table varies with T and not with t.
Includes a factor t, forcing all slopes to 0 at t=0 and making slopes change with t; the table has nonzero slopes at t=0 and no change across t.

ap_calculus_ab-m25.explanation_en: Each row of the table is constant across t, so the slope depends only on T. The slope is 1 at T=10, 0 at T=20 and -1 at T=30, which matches (20-T)/10. The equation with (T-20)/10 has the opposite sign at every point. The equation in terms of t alone would give the same slope in every row and would change from column to column, which the table does not show. The equation with the factor t would give slope 0 for all T at t=0 and would vary with t, but the table shows slopes of 1, 0, -1 at t=0 and no variation in t.

ap_calculus_ab-m25.stem: A household has a savings account that earns interest while the family makes a steady withdrawal. A slope field for the balance $B$ (in dollars) at time $t$ (in years) has the segment slopes shown in the table. The slope at a given balance is the same for every $t$. Which differential equation is consistent with the slope field?

stimulus.description: Table of slope-field segment slopes dB/dt at several balances B for a savings account, identical at every time t.

data.title: Slopes in a slope field for balance B (dollars) over time t (years), 0<=t<=10
columns: slope dB/dt (dollars per year), same for every t

options.why: Correct: gives -100, 0, 100, 200 at B=1000, 2000, 3000, 4000, matching the table.
Adds the withdrawal instead of subtracting it; gives slope 300 at B=2000, but the table shows 0.
Reverses the sign of the whole expression; gives +100 at B=1000, but the table shows -100.
Matches the zero slope at B=2000 but uses the wrong rate; gives 50 at B=3000, but the table shows 100.

ap_calculus_ab-m25.explanation_en: The slope is 0 at B=2000 and increases by 100 for each 1000 increase in B, so the slope is 0.1B plus a constant. Setting 0 = 0.1(2000) + c gives c = -200, so dB/dt = 0.1B - 200. Check: at B=1000 the slope is -100, and at B=4000 it is 200, both matching the table. The equation with +200 gives 300 at B=2000, not 0. The equation 200 - 0.1B has the opposite sign and gives +100 at B=1000. The equation 0.05B - 100 is zero at B=2000 but gives only 50 at B=3000, so its rate is too small.

ap_calculus_ab-m26.stem: In a laboratory, the concentration $C(t)$, in mg/L, of a dye in a mixing tank satisfies $\frac{dC}{dt} = -\frac{1}{2}(C-4)$ for $t \ge 0$, where $t$ is measured in minutes, and $C(0)=10$. What is $C(2\ln 3)$?

stimulus.description: Differential equation with initial condition for dye concentration in a tank.

options.why: Separates variables, integrates, uses C(0)=10 to get C=4+6e^{-t/2}, then evaluates e^{-ln3}=1/3 to get 4+2=6.
Drops the constant 4 after integrating (uses C=6e^{-t/2}), treating C-4 as the solution itself, giving 2.
Sign error in the exponent when integrating (uses e^{+t/2}), giving 4+6*3=22.
Ignores the equilibrium shift and uses C=10e^{-t/2}, giving 10/3.

ap_calculus_ab-m26.explanation_en: Separate: dC/(C-4) = -(1/2)dt, so ln|C-4| = -t/2 + k. Thus C-4 = Ae^{-t/2}. Since C(0)=10, A=6, so C=4+6e^{-t/2}. At t=2 ln 3, e^{-ln 3}=1/3, so C=4+2=6. The option 2 forgets the added 4 (it equals only the decaying part 6e^{-t/2}). The option 22 uses a positive exponent, which would make C grow away from 4, contradicting the negative rate. The option 10/3 solves as if the equilibrium were 0, ignoring the factor C-4.

ap_calculus_ab-m26.stem: A bakery owner models the book value $V$ of an oven, in thousands of dollars, $t$ years after purchase, using the information in the table. The owner plans to replace the oven when its book value reaches 15 thousand dollars. According to the model, at what time $t$ will the oven be replaced?

stimulus.description: Table of facts about a bakery oven's book value V, in thousands of dollars, t years after purchase.

options.why: Separate variables: ln V = -0.2t + C, V = 30e^{-0.2t}; setting V=15 gives e^{-0.2t}=1/2, so t = 5 ln 2.
Inverts the coefficient: divides by 5 instead of by 0.2 when solving -0.2t = -ln 2.
Treats the rate as constant (linear decay), solving 30 - 0.2t = 15, ignoring that the rate is proportional to V.
Sign error: writes ln(1/2) = ln 2 relation incorrectly and drops the negative from -0.2t, giving a negative time.

ap_calculus_ab-m26.explanation_en: Separating variables gives dV/V = -0.2 dt, so ln|V| = -0.2t + C. Using V(0)=30 gives V = 30e^{-0.2t}. Setting 30e^{-0.2t} = 15 gives e^{-0.2t} = 1/2, so -0.2t = -ln 2 and t = 5 ln 2. The option (ln 2)/5 divides by 5 instead of by 0.2. The option 75 wrongly treats the decrease as a constant 0.2 per year, but the rate is proportional to V. The option -5 ln 2 is a sign error and is also impossible, because a negative time is before the purchase.

ap_calculus_ab-m27.stem: A field team models the dissolved oxygen concentration in a pond by $C(t)=6+2\sin\left(\frac{\pi t}{12}\right)$ milligrams per liter, where $t$ is the number of hours since sunrise, for $0\le t\le 18$. Using a calculator, what is the average value of $C$ over this interval, in mg/L?

stimulus.description: Dissolved oxygen concentration model for a pond over 18 hours.

options.why: Correct: (1/18) times the integral of C from 0 to 18 equals 6.424.
Averages the endpoint values C(0)=6 and C(18)=4, confusing average value with the mean of endpoints.
Divides the integral by 12, the period of the sine term, instead of the interval length 18.
Computes the definite integral only and forgets to divide by b-a.

ap_calculus_ab-m27.explanation_en: The average value is (1/(18-0)) times the integral from 0 to 18 of C(t) dt. The integral equals 108 + (24/pi)(1 - cos(3pi/2)) = 108 + 7.639 = 115.64, so the average is 115.64/18 = 6.42 mg/L. The value 5.00 averages only the endpoint values, which ignores how C varies in between. The value 9.64 divides the integral by 12, the period, rather than the interval length 18. The value 115.64 is the integral itself and was never divided by the interval length.

ap_calculus_ab-m27.stem: A food truck's revenue rate is modeled by $R(t)=40+25\ln(t+1)$ dollars per hour, where $t$ is the number of hours since opening, $0\le t\le 8$. Which of the following is the average value of $R$ over the 8-hour shift, in dollars per hour?

stimulus.description: A food truck's revenue rate function over an 8-hour shift.

data.units: R in dollars per hour; t in hours since opening

options.why: Computes the integral (total revenue) but forgets to divide by the interval length 8.
Averages the endpoint values R(0)=40 and R(8)≈95 instead of integrating; the model is not linear, so this is wrong.
Divides the integral by 9 (the value of t+1 at the right endpoint) instead of by the interval length 8.

ap_calculus_ab-m27.explanation_en: The average value is (1/(8−0))∫0^8 (40+25 ln(t+1))dt. A calculator gives the integral ≈ 760.0, so the average is about 95.0 dollars per hour. The option 760.0 is the total revenue, not divided by 8. The option 62.5 averages the endpoint values, which does not account for the curved shape of R. The option 84.4 divides by 9 rather than by the interval length 8.

ap_calculus_ab-m28.stem: In a lab, the concentrations of two dissolved substances along a 3-cm tube are modeled by $f(x)=x^2$ and $g(x)=4x-x^2$, where $x$ is distance in cm and the graphs are shown. Which expression gives the total area of the region enclosed between the two curves for $0\le x\le 3$?

stimulus.description: Two curves on [0,3] showing concentration of two dissolved substances along a tube; the curves cross at x=2 (and meet at x=0).

options.why: Correct: splits at the intersection x=2 and uses (upper minus lower) on each piece: g-f on [0,2], f-g on [2,3].
Uses g-f over the whole interval, ignoring that the curves cross; the signed integral cancels to 0 rather than giving area.
Reverses upper and lower on each subinterval, giving negative integrands (negative area) on both pieces.
Stops at the intersection x=2 and omits the region from x=2 to x=3 that the stated interval includes.

ap_calculus_ab-m28.explanation_en: Setting x^2 = 4x - x^2 gives x=0 and x=2, so the curves cross inside [0,3]. On (0,2) g is above f, so the integrand is g-f = 4x-2x^2; on (2,3) f is above g, so the integrand is f-g = 2x^2-4x. The area is the sum of the two integrals (8/3 + 8/3 = 16/3). A single integral of g-f over [0,3] is a signed quantity that cancels to 0 and is not an area. The version with the roles reversed has the wrong sign (upper minus lower) on each piece and would give a negative value. The version using only [0,2] leaves out the region between x=2 and x=3.

ap_calculus_ab-m28.stem: A household compares two electricity plans. For $0 \le x \le 4$ months, Plan A charges at a rate of $A(x)=40+6x-x^2$ dollars per month and Plan B charges at a rate of $B(x)=40+2x$ dollars per month, as shown in the graph. The graphs intersect at $x=0$ and $x=4$. Which expression gives, and what is the value of, the extra amount the household would pay over the 4 months under Plan A compared with Plan B?

stimulus.description: Two curves on [0,4] showing monthly cost rates in dollars per month for two electricity plans; they meet at months 0 and 4, with Plan A above Plan B in between.

data.region: between curves for 0<=x<=4, Plan A above Plan B

options.why: Correct: Plan A is above Plan B on [0,4], so integrate A(x)-B(x)=4x-x^2 from 0 to 4 to get 32-64/3=32/3.
Drops the -x^2 term when subtracting, so the difference is wrongly treated as only 4x.
Uses only the quadratic term of the difference, ignoring the linear part.
Right integrand but an antiderivative/arithmetic slip (e.g., x^2/2 instead of 2x^2 for 4x), giving the wrong value.

ap_calculus_ab-m28.explanation_en: Between the intersections at x=0 and x=4, Plan A's rate is above Plan B's, so the extra cost is the area between the curves: the integral of A(x)-B(x)=4x-x^2 from 0 to 4. This equals 2x^2 - x^3/3 evaluated from 0 to 4, which is 32 - 64/3 = 32/3 dollars. The option integrating only 4x forgets the quadratic term of the difference. The option integrating only x^2 forgets the linear part. The option with value 16/3 has the correct integrand but an incorrect antiderivative, so its value is wrong.

ap_calculus_ab-m29.stem: A laboratory trough has a base in the xy-plane (units in meters) that is the region bounded by the graphs of $y=\sqrt{x}$ and $y=\frac{x}{2}$, as shown. Cross sections of the trough perpendicular to the x-axis are rectangles whose height is 3 times the length of their base in the region. Which of the following gives the volume of the trough, in cubic meters?

stimulus.description: Region in the first quadrant bounded above by y = sqrt(x) and below by the line y = x/2, between x = 0 and x = 4, shown as the base of a trough.

data.region: between the curves for 0<=x<=4; the curves intersect at (0,0) and (4,2)
data.cross_sections: perpendicular to x-axis, rectangles whose base lies in the region and whose height is 3 times the base length

options.why: Correct: the area is 3(base)^2 = 3(sqrt(x)-x/2)^2, integrated over [0,4].
Forgets the factor 3 in the height (uses base squared only).
Integrates 3 times the base length, treating the rectangle area as height times a single length rather than base times height = 3·base².
Squares the integrated base length incorrectly or mixes the rule: computes 3 times the integral of the base length times an extra factor, not the integral of the squared length.

ap_calculus_ab-m29.explanation_en: Base length is sqrt(x) - x/2 (the square root curve lies above the line on 0<x<4). Height is 3 times this, so the rectangle area is 3(sqrt(x) - x/2)^2. Volume = integral from 0 to 4 of 3(sqrt(x) - x/2)^2 dx = 1.6 m^3. The value 0.533 omits the factor of 3 in the height. The value 4.000 integrates 3 times the base length instead of base times height, so it never squares the length. The value 4.800 is also not the integral of the correct area function (it overcounts by treating the area as 9 times the squared length integral's wrong scaling).

ap_calculus_ab-m29.stem: A company designs a concrete planter whose base is the region $R$ in the figure, bounded below by $y=0.5x^2$ and above by $y=6-x$, with $x$ and $y$ in feet. Every cross section of the planter perpendicular to the $x$-axis is a rectangle with its base in $R$ and a constant height of $0.5$ foot. Which expression, and value, gives the volume of the planter in cubic feet?
ap_calculus_ab-m29.stimulus: {"kind":"graph","description":"Region R in the xy-plane (feet) between the parabola y=0.5x^2 below and the line y=6-x above, for x between the two intersection points.","data":{"x_axis":{"label":"x (feet)","min":-6,"max":4},"y_axis":{"label":"y (feet)","min":0,"max":12},"curves":[{"label":"lower boundary","equation":"y = 0.5*x^2"},{"label":"upper boundary","equation":"y = 6 - x"}],"intersections_x":[-4.606,2.606],"region":"R between the curves from x=-1-sqrt(13) to x=-1+sqrt(13)","cross_sections":"rectangles perpendicular to x-axis, base in R, constant height 0.5 ft"}

options.why: Correct: the rectangle's base is the vertical width 6-x-0.5x^2 and its height is 0.5, so area is 0.5 times the width; integrate over the full intersection interval.
Treats the rectangles as squares by squaring the width, ignoring that the height is the constant 0.5 rather than the width.
Integrates only the width, which is the area of region R, and omits the 0.5 ft height of each cross section.
Uses the wrong lower limit 0, as if the region began at the y-axis, instead of the left intersection point.

ap_calculus_ab-m29.explanation_en: Each cross section perpendicular to the x-axis has base equal to the vertical distance between the curves, 6-x-0.5x^2, and height 0.5, so its area is 0.5(6-x-0.5x^2). The curves meet where x^2+2x-12=0, at x=-1±sqrt(13), about -4.606 and 2.606. Integrating over that interval gives about 28.5 cubic feet. The squared-width integral treats the cross sections as squares, which contradicts the constant height of 0.5. The plain-width integral gives the area of R and forgets the height. The integral starting at 0 omits the part of the region to the left of the y-axis.

ap_calculus_ab-m30.stem: Water flows into a laboratory tank at rate $R(t)=4+3\sin(0.5t)$ liters per minute and drains out at rate $D(t)=2+0.1t$ liters per minute, for $0\le t\le 12$ minutes, where $t$ is in minutes. The tank contains 30 liters at $t=0$. Which expression gives the volume of water, in liters, in the tank at $t=12$, and what is its value?

stimulus.description: Rates of water flowing into and out of a laboratory tank, with the initial volume.

options.why: Correct: the final amount equals the initial amount plus the net change, the integral of inflow minus outflow.
Treats the accumulated net change as the final volume, forgetting the initial 30 liters.
Adds only the inflow to the initial volume, ignoring that water drains out.
Treats the rates at t=12 as constant over the interval instead of integrating the varying rates.

ap_calculus_ab-m30.explanation_en: Final volume equals initial volume plus the net change, and the net change is the integral of the inflow rate minus the outflow rate. That gives 30 plus about 17.04, or about 47.04 liters. Leaving out the 30 liters gives only the net change of 17.04, not the volume. Adding only the inflow ignores the draining water and overstates the volume. Multiplying the endpoint net rate by 12 wrongly treats the rates as constant, when both change over the interval.

ap_calculus_ab-m30.stem: A bakery's water tank holds 500 gallons at time $t=0$ hours. For $0\le t\le 12$, water flows into the tank at a constant rate of 30 gallons per hour and flows out at a rate of $r(t)=40+12\sin\left(\frac{\pi t}{6}\right)$ gallons per hour. How many gallons of water are in the tank at $t=12$?

stimulus.description: A bakery water tank is refilled at a constant rate and drained at a time-varying rate. The tank holds 500 gallons at t=0.

options.why: Correct: initial amount plus the integral of (inflow minus outflow) over [0,12] gives 500 - 120 = 380.
Sign error: adds the net drain of 120 to 500 instead of subtracting it.
Treats the outflow total (480) as the only change and ignores the inflow, giving 500 - 480.
Reports only the magnitude of the net change and omits the initial 500 gallons.

ap_calculus_ab-m30.explanation_en: The amount at t=12 equals the initial amount plus the accumulated net rate: $500+\int_0^{12}(30-r(t))\,dt$. The integral is $\int_0^{12}(-10-12\sin(\pi t/6))\,dt=-120-(\text{about }0)=-120$, since the sine term integrates to 0 over a full period. So the tank holds $500-120=380$ gallons. The choice of 620 adds the net drain instead of subtracting it. The choice of 20 ignores the 30 gal/hr inflow, subtracting only the 480 gallons drained. The choice of 120 gives only the net change and forgets the 500 gallons already in the tank.

ap_calculus_ab-f01.title: Reactor Inflow Rate from Unequally Spaced Readings
ap_calculus_ab-f01.stimulus: {"kind":"table","description":"Table of inflow rate R(t) in liters per minute into a reactor vessel at five times during a 12-minute run.","data":{"columns":["t (minutes)","R(t) (liters per minute)"],"rows":[[0,3.0],[2,4.2],[5,5.0],[9,4.4],[12,3.2]],"context":"R(t) is a differentiable function giving the rate at which solvent flows into a reactor vessel, 0<=t<=12. R is increasing on [0,5] and decreasing on [5,12].","units":{"t":"minutes","R":"liters per minute"}}

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Use a trapezoidal sum with the four subintervals determined by the table to approximate $\int_0^{12} R(t)\,dt$. Show the computation that leads to your answer, and interpret the value with units in context.
parts.model_answer: Trapezoidal sum = (1/2)(2)(3.0+4.2)+(1/2)(3)(4.2+5.0)+(1/2)(4)(5.0+4.4)+(1/2)(3)(4.4+3.2) = 7.2+13.8+18.8+11.4 = 51.2. Approximately 51.2 liters of solvent flowed into the reactor during the 12 minutes.

rubric_rows.criterion: Setup: uses the correct subinterval widths 2, 3, 4, 3 with the averages of the endpoint values
required_elements: (1/2)(width)(sum of endpoint values) for each subinterval

rubric_rows.criterion: Answer 51.2
Interpretation with units: total volume of solvent in liters entering over 0<=t<=12 minutes

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Find the left Riemann sum approximation of $\int_0^{12} R(t)\,dt$ using the same four subintervals. Then, using the information that R is increasing on $[0,5]$ and decreasing on $[5,12]$, determine whether the left Riemann sum applied only to the subintervals within $[0,5]$ is an overestimate or an underestimate of $\int_0^5 R(t)\,dt$. Justify your answer.
parts.model_answer: Left sum = 2(3.0)+3(4.2)+4(5.0)+3(4.4) = 51.8. On [0,5] R is increasing, so on each subinterval the left endpoint gives the minimum value of R, so the left sum there (2(3.0)+3(4.2)=18.6) is an underestimate of the integral over [0,5].

rubric_rows.criterion: Setup: left endpoint values with correct widths
Answer 51.8
Underestimate on [0,5], justified by R increasing so left endpoint values are smaller than R on each subinterval
required_elements: left endpoint gives smaller value on each subinterval
common_errors: Applies the conclusion to the whole [0,12] where R is not monotonic

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Using your trapezoidal approximation from part (a), find the approximate average rate of inflow over $0\le t\le 12$. Include units, and state what this average represents.
parts.model_answer: Average value approx (1/12)(51.2) = 4.267 liters per minute (accept 64/15). It is the constant inflow rate that would deliver the same total volume in 12 minutes.

rubric_rows.criterion: Divides the part (a) approximation by 12
Units and meaning: liters per minute; constant rate giving same total volume over the 12 minutes

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: A technician claims the left Riemann sum from part (b) must be an overestimate of $\int_0^{12} R(t)\,dt$ because 51.8 is greater than the trapezoidal value 51.2. Is the claim justified? Explain using the behavior of R.
parts.model_answer: Not justified. Comparing two approximations does not show which one is above the true value. Because R increases on [0,5] and decreases on [5,12], the left sum underestimates on [0,5] but overestimates on the decreasing portion [5,12], so the overall error direction cannot be concluded from monotonicity.

rubric_rows.criterion: States claim not justified, citing that R changes from increasing to decreasing so left-sum error has opposite directions on different parts (or that comparing two approximations does not establish the true value)
required_elements: R is increasing then decreasing / not monotonic on [0,12]
alt_solutions: Comparing two estimates does not determine the true value of the integral

ap_calculus_ab-f01.title: Fleet Fuel Use: Estimating Total Consumption from a Rate Table

stimulus.description: Table of fuel consumption rate R(t) in gallons per hour for a delivery fleet at selected times t, in hours after 6 AM.

data.context: R is a continuous, differentiable function giving the rate at which a delivery fleet uses fuel. Domain 0<=t<=8. Fuel budget for the shift: 100 gallons.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Using the subintervals given by the table, compute a left Riemann sum with 4 subintervals to approximate $\int_0^8 R(t)\,dt$. Show the terms of your sum and give the units of your answer.

rubric_rows.criterion: Setup: left endpoints with correct widths 2,1,3,2
Answer 101 with units gallons

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Using the same subintervals, compute a trapezoidal sum approximation of $\int_0^8 R(t)\,dt$. Then find the approximate average fuel consumption rate over the 8-hour shift.

rubric_rows.criterion: Setup of trapezoids with correct widths and averaged heights
Trapezoidal value 95.5
Average rate = estimate divided by 8, about 11.938 gallons per hour, with units

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: The right Riemann sum with the same subintervals is 90. A manager says, 'Since the left sum is 101 and the right sum is 90, the actual total fuel used must be between 90 and 101 gallons.' Is this conclusion justified? Explain, referring to the behavior of R shown in the table.
parts.model_answer: Not justified. Left and right sums bracket the integral only if R is monotonic on the whole interval. The table shows R increases from 12 to 15 on [0,2] and then decreases, so R is not monotonic; the actual total could lie outside [90,101].

rubric_rows.criterion: States conclusion is not justified, naming the condition that R must be monotonic (always increasing or always decreasing) for left/right sums to bound the integral
common_errors: Claims the sums always bracket the integral

rubric_rows.criterion: Uses table data: R increases from 12 to 15 then decreases, so not monotonic

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: The fleet has a fuel budget of 100 gallons for the shift. Based on your trapezoidal estimate, does the budget appear sufficient? Give one reason, using the table, why the estimate cannot guarantee the answer.
parts.model_answer: The estimate 95.5 gallons is less than 100, so the budget appears sufficient. However, the table gives R at only five times, and R rises then falls, so the trapezoidal sum could be off from the true total (the true value of the integral depends on values of R between the data points).

rubric_rows.criterion: Compares 95.5 gallons with 100 and concludes budget appears sufficient
Gives valid limitation: only discrete data, unknown behavior/concavity between points so error is not determined
required_elements: limited data points or unknown concavity between values
alt_solutions: Estimate not guaranteed because R is not known to be concave up/down on each subinterval

ap_calculus_ab-f02.title: Reservoir Depth from a Rate-of-Change Graph

stimulus.description: Piecewise-linear graph of h'(t), in meters per day, for 0<=t<=10 days, through points (0,2), (2,0), (5,-3), (7,0), (10,3).

data.units: h in meters, t in days

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: The depth of water in a reservoir at time t days is h(t), in meters, differentiable for 0<=t<=10, with h(0)=20. The graph of h' is shown in the stimulus. Find the value of t at which h has its absolute minimum on [0,10], and find that minimum value. Justify your answer.
parts.model_answer: h'=0 at t=2 and t=7. h' changes from positive to negative at t=2 (local max) and from negative to positive at t=7 (local min). Candidates: t=0,7,10. h(7)=20+2-4.5-3=14.5; h(10)=14.5+4.5=19; h(0)=20. Absolute minimum is 14.5 meters at t=7.

rubric_rows.criterion: Identifies critical points where h'=0
Justifies t=7 as local min by sign change of h' from negative to positive
Computes h(7) by net area
Compares with endpoint values h(0)=20 and h(10)=19 and concludes, with units
alt_solutions: Use the candidates test; or argue h decreases on (2,7) and increases on (7,10), with h(0)=20 > h(7), so min at t=7 (must still compare h(7) to h(0)).

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: On what intervals is the graph of h concave down? Does the graph of h have a point of inflection? Give a reason for your answers.
parts.model_answer: h'' is the slope of h'. h' is decreasing on (0,5), so h is concave down on (0,5) and concave up on (5,10). Because the concavity changes at t=5, h has an inflection point at t=5.

rubric_rows.criterion: Concave down interval
Reason: h' is decreasing on that interval (h''<0)
required_elements: h' decreasing / negative slope of h'

rubric_rows.criterion: Inflection at t=5 because concavity changes (h' goes from decreasing to increasing)

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: At what time t is the water level falling most rapidly, and at what rate? Include units and justify.
parts.model_answer: The level falls at rate -h'(t), which is largest where h' is least. The graph shows h' has its minimum value -3 at t=5, so the level falls most rapidly at t=5 at 3 meters per day.

rubric_rows.criterion: t=5 with justification from the minimum of h' on the graph
required_elements: h' is least / most negative there

rubric_rows.criterion: Rate 3 meters per day with units

ap_calculus_ab-f02.title: Smart-Thermostat Savings: Reading the Graph of S'

stimulus.description: Piecewise linear graph of S'(t), the rate of change of a household's cumulative savings in dollars per month, for 0 <= t <= 10 months, passing through (0,0), (2,6), (5,-3), (7,-3), (10,3).

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: A family enrolls in a smart-thermostat program. Their cumulative savings, in dollars, after t months is S(t), which is differentiable for 0 <= t <= 10. The graph of S' is shown and is linear between the labeled points. Find all values of t in (0,10) at which S has a local maximum or local minimum. Justify your answer.
parts.model_answer: S'(t)=0 at t=4 and t=8.5. S' changes from positive to negative at t=4, so S has a local maximum there. S' changes from negative to positive at t=8.5, so S has a local minimum there.
